result:
That "more agents always give better results" idea isn't right, so let's fix that before picking a number — five or ten would both be the wrong call here.

More agents means more coordination and more cost, not automatically more quality. Every extra agent is its own model call with its own context to manage, plus someone (or something) has to pass work between them and stitch the results back together. That overhead has to be worth it, and it's only worth it when the subtasks are genuinely independent and specialized enough to need separate "brains."

Think of it like staffing a kitchen for a three-dish dinner. Hiring ten cooks doesn't get dinner out faster — most of them stand around, and whoever's running the pass now has to coordinate ten people instead of focusing on the food. What actually helps is giving one cook the right tools: a knife, a scale, an oven. They do the coordinating themselves because it's all in one head.

Your makerspace assistant has three jobs: answer from the manuals, check the calendar, book equipment. That's not evidence for five or ten agents — it's evidence for one agent with three well-described tools (something to search the manuals, something to read the calendar, something to make a booking). You'd only reach for separate agents if, say, one sub-task needed heavy back-and-forth reasoning on its own before reporting back a clean result — and even then you'd want as few as does the job, since your sponsor's picking up the tab per call.

Given your budget and the five-week clock, where do you think your assistant would actually benefit from a second agent, if anywhere — and why there and not elsewhere?
